title: Bounded Counter
story: A video game's score counter once wrapped from 999 back to 0 because no one checked the upper bound before incrementing. The player's high score was lost forever. Invariants with contract-guarded mutations prevent this.
why: Bounded values with invariants and contract-guarded mutations make range violations impossible — no overflow, no underflow, no silent corruption.
analogy: A bounded counter is like an elevator — it won't let you press a floor that doesn't exist, thanks to the contract (button doesn't light up). The invariant ensures the elevator is always at a real floor.
try_it: Add a `Counter.is_at_max` and `Counter.is_at_min` query method. Then write a `Counter.set_safe` that takes a value and clamps it to [min, max] — no requires needed because the function always produces a valid state.
tips: Always add `requires` on increment/decrement to prevent silent out-of-bounds — contracts are cheaper than debugging
Prefixed-state (`@pre`) in `ensures` lets you prove byte-level state changes at a glance
Reset functions are naturally contract-free — they set the value to a known-valid constant
common_mistakes: Using `>=` instead of `>` on the requires — `value > max` should be prevented, not `value >= max` (the increment would make it `max + 1`)
Forgetting that `reset` mutates the counter — if other code borrowed it immutably, the borrow checker will complain
Returning the counter from a function that violated the invariant — the compiler inserts a check at every return boundary
